The Hippodrome’s central spine featured three surviving monuments that outlasted surrounding walls [PDF p. 51]. A golden tripod dedicated at Delphi in 479 B.C. stood there after the Persian defeat at Plataea [PDF p. 51]. Phocians had stolen its gold six centuries prior, yet base inscriptions remained visible to archaeologists [PDF p. 51]. Constantine contributed a porphyry column topped by a bronze Apollo from Hierapolis nearby [PDF p. 51]. He altered this statue into an imperial image by replacing its head with his own features [PDF p. 51]. This practice mirrored Roman papal actions, where Aurelius was converted into St. Peter on the Corso [PDF p. 53]. North of the Hippodrome stood Constantine’s original church dedicated to Divine Wisdom [PDF p. 53]. A wooden gallery connected St. Sophia’s west door to the palace Royal Gate for imperial access [PDF p. 53].

Constantine chose Byzantium as his capital around A.D. 328 or 329, though exact dates remain uncertain [PDF p. 54]. He consecrated the city on May 11, 330, with Christian bishops blessing the palace and St. Sophia [PDF p. 55]. Although unbaptized, Constantine ensured the new capital was explicitly Christian from its inception [PDF p. 55]. The transfer of Egyptian wheat tribute provided free corn, a powerful but demoralizing incentive for immigration [PDF p. 55]. An edict in 330 named the city New Rome, though people preferred calling it Constantinople [PDF p. 56]. Constantine died peacefully on May 22, A.D. 337, receiving baptism on his deathbed [PDF p. 57]. His realm was divided among relatives until Constantius II consolidated power through murder and war [PDF p. 57].

Around A.D. 372, Huns from beyond the Don and Volga invaded Gothic lands [PDF p. 61]. The Visigoths, led by Duke Fritigern, retreated to the Danube’s southern bank in despair [PDF p. 61]. Emperor Valens allowed them to cross if they surrendered arms and provided hostages [PDF p. 63]. Roman officials accepted bribes to let Goths keep weapons, violating imperial orders significantly [PDF p. 63]. Governor Lupicinus hoarded food supplies, forcing starving Goths to sell children for bread [PDF p. 63]. An affray at Marcianopolis led Lupicinus to attempt murdering Fritigern during a banquet [PDF p. 64]. The Goths escaped and launched raids across the Balkans, joined by runaway slaves [PDF p. 64].

The unwarlike Emperor Valens entered the field in person during the following year [PDF p. 65]. He brought great reinforcements from Asia Minor to aid his struggling forces [PDF p. 65]. The Goths forced the Balkan line and approached Adrianople in three hundred seventy-eight A.D. [PDF p. 65] Valens attacked with an army of sixty thousand men near the Gothic encampment [PDF p. 65]. However, the Goths had adopted cavalry tactics while dwelling in South Russia and Roumania [PDF p. 65]. A great body of Gothic horsemen charged the Roman flank unexpectedly during battle [PDF p. 66]. The Roman left wing collapsed under the tremendous impact of the mounted assault [PDF p. 66]. Forty thousand men fell before survivors broke out in a headlong flight from the field [PDF p. 67]. The Emperor and thirty-five commanders died on the battlefield during this fearful defeat [PDF p. 67].

The historian Ammianus Marcellinus compared this slaughter to the ancient disaster at Cannae [PDF p. 67]. Victorious Goths subsequently attacked Constantinople but failed due to its vast walls and riches [PDF p. 67]. Theodosius succeeded Valens and repaired the disaster through caution and courage combined [PDF p. 68]. He destroyed marauding bands while avoiding direct conflict with the main Gothic body [PDF p. 68]. Peace followed the death of Fritigern, as Theodosius negotiated with his successor Athanarich [PDF p. 68]. Within ten years, forty thousand Teutonic horsemen served under higher pay than Romans [PDF p. 69]. Yet this policy placed imperial command effectively in barbarian hands according to the author [PDF p. 70].

The Gothic historian Jornandes recorded King Athanarich’s awe at Constantinople’s grandeur [PDF p. 70]. This impression did not last long after Theodosius died in three hundred ninety-five A.D. [PDF p. 70] His weak sons Arcadius and Honorius inherited a dangerous political situation [PDF p. 70]. The empire suffered from centralized bureaucracy that suppressed local patriotism and rights [PDF p. 71]. Civil populations were viewed merely as tax sources by the administrative caste officials [PDF p. 71]. A professional army emerged with no sympathy for the unarmed provincial civilians it protected [PDF p. 72]. Theodosius had swamped native military elements with wholesale enlistment of Gothic war-bands [PDF p. 72]. He handed chief posts to Teutons who were often alien in blood and loyalty [PDF p. 72].

After Theodosius died, factions fought between German and Roman parties at both courts [PDF p. 73]. Stilicho dominated the West as commander-in-chief for the young Emperor Honorius [PDF p. 73]. In the East, Arcadius was weak and controlled by ministers like Rufinus initially [PDF p. 73]. A Gothic captain named Gainas murdered Rufinus before compelling further appointments for himself [PDF p. 73]. Alaric led a Visigothic revolt citing unpaid arrears to the auxiliaries as pretext [PDF p. 74]. He raided from the Danube to Greece while Stilicho blockaded him in Arcadia [PDF p. 74]. The Teutonic minister allowed Alaric to escape, leading to peace and land grants [PDF p. 74].

Alaric ruled parts of the Balkans with undisputed sway for five years thereafter [PDF p. 75]. However, Alaric invaded Italy in four hundred one instead of attacking Constantinople again [PDF p. 75] Stilicho fought hard but was executed by Honorius on charges of treason shortly after [PDF p. 75]. With Stilicho gone, Alaric moved the Visigoths into Italy to plunder at will [PDF p. 76]. Meanwhile, Gainas fell out with the eunuch Eutropius in Constantinople’s court politics [PDF p. 76]. He instigated an insurrection under Tribigild to remove his rival from power [PDF p. 76]. Eutropius fled to St. Sophia where Patriarch John Chrysostom protected him temporarily [PDF p. 76]. Arcadius banished Eutropius, but Gainas had him returned and beheaded despite promises [PDF p. 76].

Gainas brought his army to Constantinople to overawe the emperor completely [PDF p. 76]. The sudden end of Gainas’s domination resulted from a chance brawl between Goths and citizens at a city gate [PDF p. 77]. This incident triggered a general outbreak against German soldiers in Constantinople [PDF p. 77]. Seven thousand Germans died, and survivors fled across the Danube [PDF p. 77]. Gainas was subsequently beheaded by Uldes, King of the Huns [PDF p. 77]. The author notes that Fravitta, a heathen Goth, defeated Gainas in the field [PDF p. 77]. This victory freed Eastern Romans from dual threats of German kingdoms and military dictators [PDF p. 78]. Emperor Arcadius enjoyed seven years of comparative peace following these events [PDF p. 78].

Conflict arose between Empress Aelia Eudoxia and Patriarch John Chrysostom [PDF p. 78]. The empress supported Theophilus of Alexandria against the popular patriarch [PDF p. 78]. Hostilities resumed after Eudoxia erected a statue in the Augustaeum [PDF p. 79]. Chrysostom’s sermon comparing her to Herodias led to his banishment in A.D. 404 [PDF p. 79]. His supporters likely burned St. Sophia and the Senate-house in retaliation [PDF p. 79]. The author argues his deposition stemmed from moral clashes rather than ecclesiastical dogma [PDF p. 79].

Arcadius died in A.D. 408, leaving the throne to his seven-year-old son Theodosius II [PDF p. 80]. Minister Anthemius managed the administration with exceptional virtue and ability [PDF p. 80]. He secured a Persian treaty and repelled Hunnish invasions of Moesia [PDF p. 80]. Theodosius II grew into an honest but intellectually limited ruler [PDF p. 81]. His sister Pulcheria assumed regency in A.D. 414 after taking a vow of chastity [PDF p. 81]. She ruled successfully for thirty-six years as a crowned nun [PDF p. 81].

Theodosius married the pagan convert Athenais, renamed Eudocia, in A.D. 421 [PDF p. 82]. Tensions between Pulcheria and Eudocia eventually led to the empress’s exile [PDF p. 82]. The author cites a dubious tale involving an apple to explain this breach [PDF p. 82]. Historical records confirm Paulinus was executed and Eudocia retired to Jerusalem [PDF p. 83].
